Introduction - December 2009
Introduction
● 
Investors still continue to dominate as a 
number of metals have made new highs despite 
rising stocks, still poor demand outside of 
China, and a temporary lull in imports by that 
country.
● 
Despite the above, the GFMS Base Metals Index 
(BMI) has made new highs reaching a peak of 
279.3 on December 2.  The BMI averaged 267.8 
in November compared to 262.8 in October 
and 149.45 in February, the lowest monthly 
average seen this year.
● 
Aluminium displays the power of the funds 
more than most.  Despite the pending closure 
of small capacity in Italy, this will be dwarfed 
by the commissioning of new capacity in the 
Middle East.
● 
Copper’s run is better justiﬁed by the 
fundamentals.  Although exchange stocks are 
trending higher, absolute levels remain low, 
particularly once demand improves.  
● 
Signiﬁcant gains in secondary production, 
particularly in China, are contributing to the 
current oversupply position in the lead market.  
This suggests the potential for a correction, but 
wider fundamentals still look positive.
● 
As we expected, levels of close to $20,000/
tonne are not justiﬁed by the recent weakness 
in the stainless steel market, so a move back to 
around $16,000 was not a surprise.
● 
The tight supply position – currently mainly 
emanating from the small-scale Indonesian 
producers – has curbed the rise in LME 
inventories.  There are some signs that demand 
is picking up.
● 
Although zinc prices have made sharp gains, 
fundamentals have worsened due to still weak 
demand.  GFMS have increased our forecasts of 
the surplus for both 2009 and 2010. 
Funding the base metal rally
There has been no major change in the key features of the 
market over the last month.  Prices have generally moved 
higher irrespective of the fundamentals.  The GFMS Base 
Metal Index (BMI) set a new high for the year of 279.3 
on December 2,  which is double the 139.7 low seen in 
February, and it stood at 278 on December 3.  The LMEX 
currently stands at $3,214 compared to the year low of 
$1,620 in mid-February.
Exchange stocks have continued to grow reﬂecting primarily 
the delay in the recovery in base metal demand growth 
outside of China.  For some of the base metal demand 
indicators that we track, they are pointing to much slower 
year-on-year declines, and much more importantly at this 
stage of the demand cycle (i.e. a turning point) a slight 
improvement in month-on-month terms.  However, we are 
slightly surprised by the slow acceleration in demand growth 
outside of China given the generally constructive economic 
data, which is largely suggesting a recovery from a low base 
and the fact that downstream inventories are low.
China import lull should soon come to an end
Our latest research trip to China has left us fairly upbeat

dwarfed by the new capacity being commissioned in the 
Middle East. Elsewhere, the general story is one of strikes 
being resolved, and idled capacity being brought back on 
stream (volumes are not that large at the moment) and new

that they serve similar end use sectors.  It is also easier to 
turn steel production back on-stream, which has undermined 
prices.  However, perhaps the key difference between the 
price performances is the lack of investment fund activity in

Funds remain active
As we have mentioned in our earlier reports, it is very 
difﬁcult to double-guess the funds partly because they are 
by no means a homogeneous group.  However, they are 
generally retaining their long-side bias.  Many of the factors 
that encouraged them into the sector, asset diversiﬁcation, 
dollar weakness, a play on China, a play on a broader 
economic recovery and sometimes a play on the individual 
fundamentals, remain in place.  As a result, we are not 
seeing any widespread liquidation.  However given the gains 
so far the risk:reward ratio is obviously less favourable than 
it was, so we expect the funds to exert a slightly less bullish 
impact than in 2009.  However, we know a number of funds 
who have no plans to exit the sector unless the economic 
climate deteriorates.
Market outlook
We have amended our analysis of the supply-demand 
balance for the fundamentals of the nickel and zinc out 
to 2010 reﬂecting the detailed work that we undertake 
for our Three Year Quarterly Forecast.  For details on 
these reports which look out to 2012, please contact 
charlesdemeester@gfms.co.uk.  We have both markets in 
surplus next year, and have increased the estimates of the 
surplus.  This highlights the point that these prices levels will 
encourage higher output, which will largely offset the much 
stronger demand conditions that GFMS expects in 2010.  
Therefore fund support will be required to support current 
prices levels, and particularly for zinc the upside from the 
price seen in early December maybe limited.  Details of 
our quarterly and annual forecasts and our high and low 
scenarios for the metals are given in the individual sections.

Economic Indicators - November 2009
Economic Indicators
As we mentioned in the introduction the OECD leading 
indicator (the CLI) is increasingly supportive of base metals 
demand even if this has yet to ﬁlter through to underlying 
consumption.  The latest OECD CLI for September passed 
100 for the ﬁrst time in 2 years.  Encouragingly the informa­
tion for Europe was sharply higher at 102.7, which was the 
second month in a row that the index was above 100.
The OECD CLI for Europe is in line with the improvement 
in the Eurozone Economic Sentiment index, which rose to 
its highest level in 14 months in November to 88.8, up from 
86.1 in October.  Conﬁdence among businesses is improving 
more quickly than the household sector, where concerns 
remain about employment and debt.  Businesses are more 
direct beneﬁciaries of the various ﬁscal packages.
We also mentioned our fairly bullish views on China 
following a recent trip.  Again the latest data is positive for 
the base metals sector.  Chinese Industrial production was 
16.1% higher year-on-year in October, driven in part by the 
78.6% year-on-year surge in automobile production, while 
urban ﬁxed asset investment was running 33.7% above 
the corresponding period of last year over the January to 
October period.
The third quarter Indian GDP ﬁgure was upbeat rising to 
7.9 % year-on-year from 6.3% year-on-year in the previous 
three months.  It was boosted by strong government 
expenditure and higher private demand, and the economy 
may be reverting towards trend growth of around 9%, 
despite still weak external demand.

Market background
Copper prices enjoyed further increases over the course of 
November and investors were once again the driving force 
behind these gains.  The month began with prices in the 
mid-$6,000s and over the ﬁrst half copper ﬂuctuated within 
a $200 range around that level.  Boosted but an apparent 
deadlock emerging between workers and management of the 
Spence mine in Chile, prices moved decisively in the upper 
$6,000s in the second half of the month, the LME ofﬁcial 
price peaking at $6,946/tonne on the 23rd, up by 151% on 
the trough of December 2008.  Prices have continued their 
uptrend above $7,000/tonne in early December, even though 
the aforementioned issues at Spence mine were resolved.
Contradicting its price performance (and thus conﬁrming 
our contention that investors remained in the driving seat), 
copper’s apparent fundamentals were once again uninspiring 
over the course of November.  LME inventories rose by a 
further 68,825 tonnes to 441,000 tonnes, bringing the year-
to-date net increase to 100,450 tonnes, and growth was also 
recorded in other exchange inventories.  Although lagged, 
the latest data available on Chinese imports continues to 
suggest that these are declining and by implication putting 
apparent consumption under pressure (even though real 
end-use demand is probably still growing).  Elsewhere, the 
signs are overwhelmingly suggesting of no material recovery 
having commenced in the mature economies.
Spence strike ends as wage talks resume
Ending one of the longest strikes in South American mining 
history, unions and owners of Chile’s Spence copper mine 
agreed to resume wage negotiations on 20th November.  In 
addition to the return of the Spence mine, output in which 
will return to normal levels by January, boosting production, 
this development also provides some relief to fears of other 
similar disruptions taking place in the region.  For instance, 
just before the commencement of the new wage negotiations 
was announced, a Chilean mine union had threatened to halt 
output at other mines owned by BHP Billiton, in solidarity 
with Spence workers.
Added to the developments at Spence and the successful 
outcome of wage negotiations between BHP and miners at 
Escondida in October, another potential threat to production 
was recently removed as workers at the Antamina operation 
in Peru announced a deal had been reached.  The union, that 
had previously voted to go on strike, reached an agreement 
with the owners, BHP Billiton, Xstrata, Teck and Mitsubishi, 
on 25th November.
All the above can by no means guarantee that frictions will 
be avoided in the course of upcoming negotiations for the 
series of labour contracts that are set to expire over the next 
few months in the area (Chile-Peru), as well as elsewhere.  
Nevertheless, evidence of both miners and operators 
being prepared to compromise suggests these risks are 
manageable.  GFMS’ own projections are conditional on 
such disruptions being contained, although not altogether 
disappearing.
Production growth remains positive
With key downside risks to global production removed 
as Escondida, Spence and Antamina labour disputes are 
resolved, copper mine production seems set to continue 
growing, albeit at a relatively slow pace.  We note that 
WBMS production ﬁgures over the last few months to 
September see levels averaging above 1.3 million tonnes per 
month, compared to the February trough of less than 1.2 
million tonnes.  Rising utilisation rates as well as genuine 
capacity growth have both contributed to this trend.  This 
saw global production over the ﬁrst nine months of the year 
increase by more than 2% according to the WBMS, despite 
losses suffered due to technical difﬁculties, labour-related 
disruptions as well as, at the margin, price related cutbacks 
early in the year.

The latest relevant news releases suggest that positive 
growth rates, at least on a year-on-year basis, have been 
maintained through to the present time.  In Chile, ofﬁcial 
statistics indicate copper mine production was up nearly 
10% year-on-year in October, at 496,217 tonnes, even 
though year-to-date output was virtually unchanged.  In 
Zambia, for which WBMS data for the third quarter seems 
to be estimated rather than actual, First Quantum Minerals 
announced that production and the Kansanshi operation in 
the third quarter was up by 15% year-on-year to 61,300 
tonnes.
Considering the outlook for copper mining, capacity 
expansion plans as well as efforts to improve utilisation 
continue, as prices ﬂoat at levels close to twice their 
estimated average marginal production cost.  The latest 
major announcement on this front was Chile’s Codelco 
nearing completion of one of the world’s largest conveyor 
belts, connecting its Chuquimata and Radomiro Tomic mines 
and boosting combined production capacity by 160,000 
tonnes per year.  
Demand conditions yet to improve in mature 
economies
Against the backdrop of growing production, we have yet 
to see evidence of consumption recovery outside China.  
Despite global economic indicators being positive for a 
number of months, the latest WBMS release suggests that 
demand excluding China over the few months to September, 
averaging in the mid-900,000 tonnes, was still signiﬁcantly 
lower than the norm over the last few years.  Consumption 
in Europe has been particularly disappointing, even failing 
to post noteworthy month-on-month gains recently.  In 
Japan, although the country’s Copper and Brass Association 
said that rolled copper products output rose for the seventh 
consecutive month in October, the 67,927 tonne ﬁgure was 
still down a hefty 12.4% year-on-year.
Chinese imports continue to fall but stocks may be 
reaching ‘equilibrium’ levels
After a surprising increase in September, Chinese reﬁned 
copper imports returned to their downward trajectory 
in October, falling by 45% month-on-month to just over 
150,000 tonnes.  This prompted an 18% fall in apparent 
consumption compared to September.  Looking at semis 
production data, October was only marginally lower than 
September.  On a year-on-year basis, October was the ﬁrst 
month this year yet when the growth in semis production 
exceeded that in apparent consumption.
The mismatch between the trends in real - proxied by semis 
production - and apparent consumption noted in October (as 
well as also in August) is the mirror image of the situation 
earlier this year, when apparent consumption growth was 
faster than semis output growth.  During that time, although 
we had acknowledged that this ‘paradox’ related in part 
relate to lower scrap availability as well as SRB purchases, 
GFMS had argued that much of the ‘excess’ material had 
found its way into unreported inventories.  In contrast, 
the recent reversal of conditions will almost certainly have 
seen the aforementioned unreported inventories decline.  
This would have been augmented by the persistently tight 
scrap market.  We note that scrap imports into China fell by 
36% month-on-month in October to their lowest level since 
February.
An interesting question, at this point, is how long the stock 
depletion will last.  Two key factors will affect this, assuming 
‘real’ demand keeps to levels similar to those the last eight 
months of semis production data point to: the net increase in 
unreported inventories that took place since the ﬁnal quarter 
of 2008 and the ‘equilibrium’ level of unreported inventories 
for the Chinese market.

Market outlook
Entering the ﬁnal month of the year, copper’s fundamentals 
remain uninspiring and prima facie worsening.  The much 
anticipated recovery in consumption outside China to-date 
has been limited and more material gains now seem set 
to kick in well into 2010.  In regards to China, the market 
may have to absorb news of lower imports in November 
and December; however GFMS expects that the strength 
of imports will return in early 2010.  Against this backdrop, 
fears of supply disruptions are easing, as key potential 
disputes have now been resolved.  Finally, as publicly 
available data and anecdotal information alike suggest that 
speculative positions are at historical highs, the risks for 
liquidations taking place seem signiﬁcant.
Due to the above, our short-term expectations under our 
Base Case see copper prices experience a correction before 
the end of the year.  Moreover, as one can see in the table 
below, are projections for the ﬁrst few months of the year 
see current levels being the top of a rather volatile market.  
Nevertheless, we acknowledge that investor sentiment 
towards the market will almost certainly remain positive and 
that this will tend to skew prices towards the upper end of 
the range.  Although we believe that visits well below the 
$6,000/tonne mark cannot be ruled out, these will almost 
certainly be very brief.  This is also reﬂected in our average 
quarterly forecast of $6,700/tonne.
As consumption accelerates from the second quarter 
onwards, prices are expected to develop some additional 
momentum, particularly later in the year, when the market 
moves into deﬁcit.  Although volatility is maintained 
throughout, prices trend upwards over the rest of the year.
Due to our Base Case, described above, being relatively 
bullish, the scope for a materially different more bullish 
Scenario B is limited.  Under such assumptions as a rapid 
recovery in consumption commencing very early in the 
new year and affecting all regions, the market could move 
into deﬁcit as early as the second quarter.  Current levels 
could prove a starting point for a rally that could see prices 
average as high as $8,000/tonne by the ﬁnal quarter of 
next year.  In contrast, under the assumption of a sluggish 
recovery, as the private sector fails to successfully take 
control of the economy after the stimulus packages run out 
of steam, and particularly given the limited scope for further 
intervention by governments, prices could easily slump 
towards their marginal costs of production, before the end of 
2010.

Market background
Nickel prices continued their downward trend that 
commenced in late October touching just over a four month 
low to below $16,000/tonne in early December.  The cash 
price fell by a notable $650 in the space of one day, which 
resulted from problems in equity markets. Prices remain 
subject to further weakness, however as demand for 
stainless steel continues to dwindle.  
Inventories on the LME, as a result, have continued to climb 
and are only 8,500 tonnes off from the historical high of 
151,254 tonnes hit in November 1994.  In our view, this 
upward trend will continue into the New Year as we not only 
await a demand-side recovery, but additionally the market 
will have to absorb higher production from the 60,000 
tonnes per year Goro project and from China’s nickel pig 
iron producers.  A more recent threat for prices however, is 
the potential for China’s privately held stocks to be released 
before the end of the year, some of which is expected to end 
up in LME warehouses.  
China remains the key demand driver
According to the World Bureau of Metals Statistics (WBMS), 
global nickel demand registered positive growth in 
September, which combined with previous monthly gains 
saw the year-to-date total decline by just 0.3% year-on-
year.  Of course this decline represents a vast improvement 
in comparison to the year-to-date falls noted in previous 
months, but notably it has solely been driven by China.  
Consumption elsewhere has remained lacklustre, or arguably 
has worsened after looking at their individual stainless 
markets.
The WBMS estimates that China accounted for 44% of global 
demand in the ﬁrst nine months of the year in comparison to 
almost half of that in the year-earlier period.  Importantly, 
the country saw its (apparent) consumption of nickel grow 
by some 89% year-on-year, largely the result of its excessive 
importing earlier in the year.  Real consumption however 
is much lower, as can be deduced with Antaike’s latest 
forecast of growth of 37.6% this year.  The projection is 
based on 32% growth in stainless steel production, which 
the organisation believes will reach 9.7 million tonnes by 
the end of this year.  Furthermore, 46% of this total will be 
accounted for by the 300-series, 30% from the 200-series 
and 24% from 400 grades of stainless steel.  Looking ahead, 
Antaike estimates real nickel demand growth will slow 
dramatically to just 5.1% in 2010 to reach 470,000 tonnes.  
Weak stainless demand will continue seeing prices 
lower
As noted in our previous monthly report, stainless mills in 
China curbed output in response to the huge inventory that 
had been built up.  While the effect of these cutbacks has 
seen Chinese prices rise temporarily, GFMS have doubts 
about the sustainability of this improvement.  Not only is 
stainless steel demand weak but reportedly many mills 
remain with more than sufﬁcient stock.  As a result, prices 
of East Asian-origin 304 stainless cold rolled sheets for 
December delivery have fallen to a range of RMB 17,100-
17,600/tonne from November’s range of RMB 17,500-
17,900/tonne.  
Recent reports suggest that Posco is likely to trim its 
domestic prices for December delivery after retaining its 
prices in November.  Softer nickel prices, poor demand and 
rising stock levels are all behind the expected price cut.  
Meanwhile, production of stainless at Posco in October fell by 
around 3% compared with September.  We believe that there 
is scope for lower output during the remainder of the year.

A similar situation prevails in Europe and North America.  
Base prices for December delivery are down on the previous 
month by 4.3% and 4.1%, respectively, while the alloy 
surcharge, based on the nickel price, in Europe is down 
by 2.7%, however up by almost 4.0% in North America.  
Outokumpu’s alloy surcharge on type 304 austenitic material 
is virtually unchanged at €1,005/tonne, but both austenitic 
316 and ferritic 430 coil are down by about 5% month-on-
month at €1,547/tonne and €246/tonne, respectively.  
Global production remains low
In terms of supply, global reﬁned production up to 
September fell by the same level as in the ﬁrst eight months, 
notably 3.4% year-on-year.  The Americas continued to 
register the steepest decline on lower output in Canada, 
which has been due to the strike at Vale.  The only region 
that saw growth however was Asia.  Within this, China 
experienced growth of 39.1% year-on-year, which indeed 
takes into account higher nickel pig iron production.  More 
recent data by the China Nonferrous Metals Industry 
Association (CNI-A), suggests Chinese reﬁned production at 
132,000 tonnes up to October was up by almost 25% year-
on-year.  It should be noted that this ﬁgure does not take 
into account nickel pig iron production, however is primarily 
because of higher output at Jinchuan.  The company has 
been maintaining output between 10-12,000 tonnes per 
month since the start of the year.  
However, there is some evidence emerging that growth in 
Chinese nickel pig iron production.  It has been reported 
that some of these producers have paused their production 
for over a month because of the falling nickel prices.  More 
importantly, China’s imports of nickel ore and concentrates, 
which have increased sharply in recent months, fell by 
51.8% on September.  However, it is understood that this 
could largely be due to the monsoon season that lies ahead 
in Southeast Asia (where the ore and concentrate comes 
from), which means mining and transporting the material 
becomes difﬁcult.  
Chinese imports halve in October
Chinese imports of reﬁned nickel continued the downward 
trend that started following the record high in July.  The 
CNI-A estimates imports fell by almost 50% month-on-
month in October to 11,300 tonnes as higher LME prices in 
comparison to the domestic price made it less proﬁtable to 
import.  Nevertheless, year-to-date imports remained robust 
compared to the year-earlier period.  Going forward, with the 
nickel price looking as if it will fall further, we expect Chinese 
imports to pick up in the coming months as investors will 
look to take advantage of the arbitrage.  In contrast, exports 
in the country soared to 5,900 tonnes in October increasing 
by 86.3% on September as the price gap between the two 
exchanges widened.
Nickel projects have been delayed
While the 60,000 tonnes per year Goro project is set to 
come online, there are now a few projects that have been 
delayed.  Zambia’s 10,000 tonnes per year Munali mine 
will delay restarting production to early 2010 from October 
this year due to negotiations over working capital with 
a Chinese bank.  It is expected the concentrate will be 
supplied to China’s Jinchuan.  Similarly, production from the 
31,000 tonnes per year Ramu nickel mine in PNG will be 
delayed until June 2010, which was previously expected to 
commence at the start of next year.  Nickel from the mine is 
designed to supply stainless steel mills in China.

Market outlook
GFMS have revised our supply-demand balance and now 
forecast a higher surplus both this year and in 2010, 
although the trend remains the same.  We have factored in a 
smaller disruption allowance for 2009 as opposed to a larger 
one previously, and assumed slightly higher production, 
while little has changed in the way we view the demand-side 
of the market.  We are projecting a surplus of 58,000 tonnes 
this year.  
Moving forward, the ﬁrst half of 2010 sees the uninspiring 
fundamentals persist, as stainless mills adjust production 
to what now is a less than stellar recovery in demand for 
stainless products and also due to the restocking seen earlier 
this year and to some extent through to the present time, 
running out of steam. Surpluses are seen in both the ﬁrst 
and second quarters of the year; although towards the end 
of it we expect the market will be close to balance. A swing 
to deﬁcit - albeit small in magnitude - is forecast for the 
third and fourth part of the year, as stainless production 
in mature markets reclaims part of its previous losses 
compounding ongoing growth in developing economies. Help 
is also provided by the fact that output growth fails to grow 
as fast as planned, given the uncertainty concerning the 
next generation of HPAL projects and delays at some new 
capacities. Overall, a surplus of 23,000 tonnes is forecast for 
2010.
In terms of prices, the worsening of the market’s 
fundamentals in the ﬁrst quarter will see prices test lower 
levels than during this quarter, although ongoing investor 
interest will, in our view, rule out a return to levels near 
those recorded in the aftermath of the crisis, as well as

Cobalt
Market background
After holding at $20/lb for much of November, the price of 
99.3% material slid in early December as trading was thin 
and sellers had to reduce their numbers to secure business.  
Volatile prices have more recently been met with widening 
ranges on December 4 as low grade cobalt traded at $18.25-
19.15/lb from $18.45-19/lb previously.  Traders at present 
are unsure of where the market is heading. 
High grade 99.8% cobalt also saw similar volatility, with 
prices picking up to $22/lb in November before dipping to 
$19.93/tonne in early December.  However the ranges in 
early December remained more stable than in the low grade 
market.
This volatility has been partly due to anticipation ahead of 
the end-February 2010 launch of the cobalt LME contract.  
Higher prices had been driven by strong demand for Russian 
material (99.3%) as a number of ﬁnancial institutions were 
in the market for physical material prior to the LME launch.  
Regarding the exchange contract, the ﬁrst long-term 
physical cobalt contract using an LME pricing formula has 
been ﬁnalised between Votorantim Metais Brazil and LN 
Metals International. This came as the LME conﬁrmed that 
Votorantim, Jinchuan Group and Sumitomo Metal Mining Co 
have applied to have their cobalt listed as an LME brand. 
Thus far only Vale Inco has registered its brand with the 
exchange.
Demand strength largely emanating from Asia
We have noted buying interest from Japanese and Chinese 
consumers in particular.  Antaike has estimated that China’s 
real consumption of cobalt will rise 2% in 2009 to 15,500 
tonnes, and 2010 consumption could potentially rise further 
as the global economy improves.  However, stocks on the 
Chinese market have risen considerably on a large rise in 
imports.
In the Far East, most of the improvement in demand is 
emanating from the battery market.  In Europe and North 
America, where the superalloys sector has a greater share of 
consumption, demand conditions are less buoyant.
Supply to increase on new projects 
The market has also been supported by the on-going strike 
at Vale Inco’s Sudbury and Voisey’s Bay operations.  At this 
stage, there is no resolution in sight to the dispute that 
began in July.  
Its effects will however be dampened by signiﬁcant increases 
at other operations.  Chambishi Metals restarted production 
at its cobalt plant in mid November after shutting in 
December 2008 on low prices.  It is planning to have metal 
available for the market at the turn of the year.  Chambishi 
has conﬁrmed that feed for the plant will come from Camec’s 
operations.
